title: Glasshouse and Weather
premise: Wren Crane, once the conservatory's celebrated prodigy, returns a decade after a public breakdown to work as its janitor, hiding in plain sight among the glasshouses they were raised in. When Ilse Marchetti, the dying last speaker of Vessic—a language Wren's grandmother helped suppress—asks Wren to become her final student, Wren must choose between protecting the conservatory's founding family, who employ and shelter them, and recording the truth of what that family destroyed. As Ilse's health fails and the board moves to demolish her cottage for an expansion, Wren secretly transcribes the language while confronting their own complicity and grief. The novel ends with Ilse's death, Wren reading the Vessic elegy aloud at the conservatory's centennial—out loud, named, unhidden—and accepting both inheritance and loss: the language survives only as memory, but so does Wren's honesty.
about_author: Lena Vane is the pen name of a former botanical garden archivist who spent seven years cataloguing endangered-language recordings before turning to fiction. Glasshouse and Weather is her second novel, written in a rented flat above a seed library.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren mops the conservatory floors at dawn, invisible among visitors who once watched them perform here as a child. Establishes the routine, the shame, the careful anonymity. Emotional beat: quiet self-erasure, comforted and suffocated by it.

chapters.title: Moss on the North Wall
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A maintenance order flags the old cottage on the grounds for inspection; Wren learns it belongs to Ilse Marchetti, whom everyone calls a relic. First glimpse of Ilse through a window, tending plants in rows like sentences. Beat: curiosity stirring under numbness.

chapters.title: What the Board Wants
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, with overheard dialogue. Director Hal Crane—Wren's uncle—announces the centennial expansion; the cottage sits where the new wing will rise. Wren says nothing. Beat: the first small betrayal by silence.

chapters.title: Ilse Speaks
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Sent to deliver an eviction notice, Wren is caught by Ilse, who greets them in Vessic—the language Wren half-remembers from lullabies. Ilse recognizes the Crane face instantly. Beat: recognition as exposure.

chapters.title: A Grammar of Refusal
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren refuses Ilse's invitation to learn, citing duty to the family. Flashback fragments: grandmother Ada Crane's role in the 1960s 'modernization' that scattered Vessic speakers. Beat: guilt surfacing.

chapters.title: Weather Report
chapters.summary: POV shift: Ilse. Ilse writes a letter she won't send, assessing Wren like weather approaching—predictable, delayed, inevitable. She begins preparing lessons anyway. Beat: patient hope.

chapters.title: The Night Shift
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Unable to sleep, Wren returns to the cottage at night and asks, barely audibly, what the word for forgiveness is. Ilse answers with a lesson instead. Beat: the door opens.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Informal lessons begin: numbers, names, the Vessic way of speaking about rain. Wren hides notebooks inside mop buckets. Beat: furtive joy.

chapters.title: Hal's Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hal shows Wren the family archive, framing Ada as a savior who gave the conservatory its land. Wren sees gaps in the story where Ilse's people should be. Beat: loyalty beginning to chafe.

chapters.title: Sofia
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Sofia Reyes, a young botanist, notices Wren's strange notes and guesses there's more to the janitor than mops. An uneasy friendship forms. Beat: being seen against one's will.

chapters.title: The Word for House
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse teaches the Vessic word for house—which also means 'the thing that holds weather.' She tells the first story of eviction, 1961, gently. Beat: history entering the room.

chapters.title: Centennial Preparations
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The expansion accelerates; demolition date set for after the centennial gala. Hal asks Wren to speak at the ceremony as 'a Crane returning.' Beat: the trap of honor.

chapters.title: Ilse Falls
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finds Ilse collapsed in the greenhouse row; hospital visit reveals a failing heart, months perhaps. The doctor mentions hospice. Beat: time becomes finite.

chapters.title: Lessons Against the Clock
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Lessons intensify—syntax, songs, the elegy form called the vesh. Ilse insists Wren learn to say goodbye properly, in Vessic, out loud. Beat: urgency braided with tenderness.

chapters.title: Ada's Letters
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the archive, Wren finds Ada's private letters admitting the 'relocation' was coerced and the recordings suppressed deliberately. Beat: the inheritance revealed as theft.

chapters.title: Confrontation Deferred
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren nearly confronts Hal, then retreats when he warmly offers Wren a curatorship—redemption on his terms. Beat: temptation of comfortable silence.

chapters.title: Sofia's Question
chapters.summary: Sofia's POV. Sofia discovers the demolition will destroy undocumented heirloom plants from Ilse's garden and challenges the board publicly. Wren stays silent again. Beat: mirror held up to cowardice.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse asks Wren to record her speaking Vessic—not for archives, but for one listener someday. Wren realizes they may be the last student ever. Beat: weight of singularity.

chapters.title: Rain in Two Languages
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A storm floods the conservatory; Wren and Ilse save the seed collection together through the night, trading words and stories. Beat: intimacy, partnership, joy.

chapters.title: Hal Suspects
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hal finds a Vessic notebook and confronts Wren coldly: sentiment threatens the family legacy and the funding tied to the gala. He gives Wren an ultimatum. Beat: pressure applied.

chapters.title: The Broken Lesson
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse senses Wren's distraction and fear; a lesson collapses into argument about whether truth or loyalty comes first. Ilse: 'A language dies of politeness first.' Beat: rupture.

chapters.title: Week of Silence
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren stops visiting, throws themselves into janitorial perfection, scrubs the past away tile by tile. Sofia watches with disappointment. Beat: regression, self-punishment.

chapters.title: The Hospital Letter
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A nurse delivers Ilse's letter—the one from chapter 6, finally sent. It contains no reproach, only the vesh elegy's opening lines and a single question: whose voice will carry it? Beat: summons.

chapters.title: Return to the Cottage
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren returns; Ilse, weaker, resumes teaching without comment. They agree to finish the elegy together before the centennial. Beat: reconciliation without absolution.

chapters.title: The Archive Theft
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren copies Ada's letters, planning to make them public at the gala. Sofia agrees to help preserve Ilse's plants. Alliances form. Beat: commitment, point of no return.

chapters.title: Hal's Offer Again
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hal, unaware, promotes Wren publicly for the gala program—naming them heir to the Crane legacy. Wren accepts with a smile that costs everything. Beat: dramatic irony tightens.

chapters.title: Vesh
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse teaches the full elegy form: a song for endings that must be spoken aloud to count. She confesses her own failure—she stayed silent for sixty years too. Beat: mutual forgiveness begun.

chapters.title: The Last Full Lesson
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A day of teaching that feels like a whole life: grammar, jokes, recipes, insults, love-words. Ilse tires quickly now. Beat: fullness shadowed by ending.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The board moves the demolition up—before the gala. Sofia's petition fails. Ilse must leave the cottage within days. Beat: stakes sharpened, injustice concrete.

chapters.title: Packing a Life
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren helps Ilse pack; every object carries a Vessic name. Ilse gives Wren her mother's dictionary, the only one. Beat: transmission of inheritance.

chapters.title: Night Before the Gala
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse, moved to a care home, rehearses nothing; she trusts. She writes Wren's name into the language itself, coining a word meaning 'the one who came back.' Beat: blessing.

chapters.title: Centennial Morning
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The gala begins; donors, press, the Crane name everywhere. Wren holds two speeches in one pocket: the one Hal wrote, and the truth. Beat: held breath.

chapters.title: The Speech
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At the podium, Wren abandons Hal's script, reads Ada's letters aloud, names the evicted families, and speaks the vesh elegy's first lines in Vessic. Uproar. Beat: climax—truth out loud.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Hal disowns Wren; some staff applaud, some walk out; Sofia organizes preservation of the cottage garden. The demolition pauses under public scrutiny. Beat: consequences, costly but clean.

chapters.title: The Call
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The care home calls: Ilse is fading fast. Wren runs through rain to her bedside. Beat: race against silence.

chapters.title: Goodbye Properly
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren speaks the complete vesh elegy at Ilse's bedside; Ilse corrects one word, smiles, and answers with the farewell formula—then quietly dies. Beat: emotional climax, goodbye said fully.

chapters.title: The Empty Cottage
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren walks the saved cottage alone, speaking Vessic to empty rooms, hearing echoes answer in memory. Grief without regret. Beat: mourning made habitable.

chapters.title: What Remains
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Months later: the conservatory opens a small Vessic room with Ilse's recordings, Sofia's plants, and the dictionary under glass. Wren teaches a children's class of six. Beat: inheritance honored, not owned.

chapters.title: Tenant No Longer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Hal sends a curt letter—neither forgiveness nor refusal; Wren files it unread in the drawer of unfinished things. Wren signs a lease on their own small flat nearby. Beat: independence, loose threads left honest.

chapters.title: Weather Holding
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, closing. Dawn at the conservatory; Wren still cleans floors, but now also teaches, and greets visitors in two languages. Final line of the elegy spoken aloud to the glasshouse light. Beat: resolution—visible, voiced, at home.
